A network whose branches shrink by R_L and turn by θ is carried onto itself by one complex multiplication, a = e^(iθ)/R_L, about the fixed point z*. Take the logarithm and that multiplication becomes a translation by (−ln R_L, θ). Every panel here is that same translation. Panel 1 slides the camera one scale step into the network; panel 2 slides the pattern along the lattice vector; panel 3 slides the flood wave along log time, because a basin RL times longer responds RL times slower; panel 4 slides a comb of partials along log frequency, which is a Shepard–Risset tone. Set the rate to zero and all four stop on the same frame.

The spacing is RL, not an octave. At RL = 2 the tone is the familiar one. At Horton's measured 2.2 the interval is a stretched octave of about 1365 cents, and the illusion still works: you are hearing the basin's own ratio. Defaults are Buck Creek, California (Rb = 3.67, RL = 2.2) as reported by Tarboton.

The network here is exactly self-similar, which real ones are not: Horton's ratios hold on average over a finite range of scales, channel velocity is only roughly scale-invariant, and measured streamflow spectra are broadly power-law rather than exactly log-periodic. The idealisation is what makes the four panels line up to the pixel.
